la:verb:corrigo.html:
cor-rĭgo (conr-), rexi, rectum, 3, v. a.
rego
,
to make straight, set right, bring into order.
Lit. (rare): catenas,: alicui digitum,: verbaque correctis incidere talia ceris,smoothed out, erased,: corpus informe gibbo, Aug. ap. : vulvas conversas,; cf.: malas labentes,: cursum (navis),; cf.: se flexus (fluminum),.—
Prov.: curva,to attempt to make crooked straight,; .—Far more freq. and class.,
Trop., to improve, amend, correct, make better, reform, restore, make good, compensate for, etc.
In gen.
With acc.: aliquem corruptum ad frugem corrigere,: gnatum mi,: ita mutat, ut ea, quae corrigere volt, mihi quidem depravare videatur,: praeterita magis reprehendi possunt quam corrigi,: tarditatem cursu, (15 a), 2: errorem paenitendo, id. Fragm. ap. ; ; cf. mendum,: delicta,: mores (opp. corrumpere),; and, mores (with vitia emendare),: acceptam in Illyrico ignominiam,: quicquid corrigere est nefas,: dum resque sinit, tua corrigo vota,: moram celeri cessataque tempora cursu,: ancipitis fortuna temporis maturā virtute correcta,: ut tibi sit qui te conrigere possis,: paterer vos ipsā re conrigi, quoniam verba contemnitis,: tu ut umquam te corrigas?: tota civitas corrigi solet continentiā,: aliā ratione malevolus, aliā amator corrigendus,; : conscius mihi sum ... corrigi me posse,.—Esp. freq. of improving, correcting an (oral or written) discourse, Müll.; , B, 2; ; ; and of the orator who employs the figure correctio (v. s. v. II.): cum corrigimus nosmet ipsos quasi reprehendentes,. —
Absol.: se fateri admissum flagitium: sed eosdem correcturos esse,; cf. .—
In medic. lang., to heal, cure: lentigines,: maciem corporis,: cutem in facie,.—Hence, cor-rectus (conr-), a, um, P. a., improved, amended, correct (very rare): ut is qui fortuito deliquit, attentior fiat correctiorque,.—Hence, subst.: correctus, i, m., one who is reformed: nihil officiunt peccata vetera correcti,.

cor-rŭo (conr-), ŭi, 3, v. n. and a.

To fall together, fall or tumble down, fall, sink to the ground, etc. (class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.: tabernae mihi duae corruerunt,; cf.: aedes corruerunt,: triclinium supra convivas,: quicquid superstruxeris corruet,: quid labefactum viribus ignis,; cf.: arbor labefacta Ictibus innumeris,; so, arbor,: statuae equestres, et saep.: paene ille timore, ego risu conrui, (10), 2: nec corruit ille, Sed retinente manum moriens e poste pependit,; so, exspirantes corruerunt,; cf. : morbo comitiali,: in vulnus,: haedus ante focos, cf. sq.—
Trop.: si uno meo fato et tu et omnes mei conruistis,: quanto altius elatus erat, eo foedius corruit,: Lacedaemoniorum opes,: Antiochea ista universa,.—Of actors: ii mihi videntur fabulam aetatis peregisse, nec tamquam inexercitati histriones corruisse,.—In a cause in court, to fail, .—
To fall, to rush headlong (very rare): quo cum corruit haec vis,: accipitres velut rostris inter se corruerent, were falling upon each other (al. leg. concurrerent), .— Impers.: longe violentius semper ex necessitate quam ex virtute corruitur,the onset is made,.—

Lit.: hanc rerum summam,: corpus,: divitias,to heap up,: corbes ab eo quod eo spicas aliudve quid corruebant, Müll.—*

la:noun:corpus.html:
corpus, ŏris, n.
cf. Sanscr. kar-, to make; Lat. creo
,
any object composed of materials perceptible by the senses, body, substance (opp. anima and animus; cf. the definition in pr.).
Lit. (very frequent in every period and species of composition).
In gen., a body, whether living or lifeless: tangere aut tangi nisi corpus nulla potest res,: animi voluptates et dolores nasci fatemur e corporis voluptatibus et doloribus, etc.,; cf. : vita, quae corpore et spiritu continetur,: parvissima quaeque Corpora constabunt ex partibus infinitis,: ignea rerum,: terraï,: acerbum Neptuni,: aquae, et saep.—Poet., plur. for sing.: nudabant corpora (nymphae) venti,; (cf. σώματα, Soph. Elec. 1232).—
In partic.
The flesh of animal bodies: ossa subjecta corpori,; cf. , prooem. § 24; 12, 10, 5: amittere,to become poor, lean,; ; cf.: abiit corpusque colorque,; and the opp. facere,to become fat, to thrive,; cf.: quo cibo fecisti tantum corporis,.—In a play upon words: inque omni nusquam corpore corpus erat,.—
Transf., the wood under the bark of a tree, .—Of discourse: nervis illis, quibus causa continetur, adiciunt superinducti corporis speciem,the covering, integument,; : corpus eloquentiae facere,the substance, the most essential part,; cf.: corpus orationis enervatur,.—
A lifeless body, a corpse, ; ; et saep.; ; —In a double sense, Halm.—Poet., the souls of the dead, the shades or departed spirits, ; .—
As opposed to the head, the trunk, .—
In mal. part., the body, person: usuram ejus corporis cepit sibi,: illa quae corpus puplicat volgo suum,; ; cf.: corpore quaestum facere,; v. quaestus.— Hence also,the testicles,; .—
Periphrastically for the individual, the person (esp. poet., to suggest that which is physically admirable or excellent; also freq. in the histt.): delecta virum corpora,; cf.: lectissima matrum,: quo pulchrior alter non fuit, excepto corpore Turni,; 11, 690: septena quot annis Corpora natorum,: ultor vestrae, fidissima corpora, mortis,; : sororum,; : conjugum vestraque ac liberorum vestrorum,; et saep.: uti corpora nostra ab injuriā tuta forent,; ; : qui liberum corpus (sc. Virginiam) in servitutem addixissent,; so, liberum,; ; ; .—Of animals: corpora

magna boum, heads, : seu quis Pascit equos ... Corpora praecipue matrum legat,; : pro tribus corporibus triginta milia talentum auri precatur accipias,.—

Meton., a whole composed of parts united, a body, frame, system, structure, community, corporation, etc.; of ships,the framework,.—Of fortifications: totum corpus coronā militum cingere,.—Of a land: Sicilia dirempta velut a corpore majore,.—Of the state: alterum (praeceptum Platonis), ut totum corpus rei publicae curent, nec dum partem aliquam tuentur, reliquas deserant,: quae (multitudo) coalescere in populi unius corpus poterat,; cf. ; and: nullum civitatis,a political body,; ; ; : totum corpus Macedoniae,; : sui corporis regem creari,: corpus mercatorum,guild,: corpori valido caput deerat (sc. exercitui dux),: oriundi ab Sabinis sui corporis creari regem volebant,; cf. ; : fabrorum et naviculariorum,: utros ejus habueris libros ... duo enim sunt corpora ... an utrosque, nescio, (13), 4; so of a book, ; ; ; ; cf.: corpus omnis Romani juris,; hence, Corpus Juris,title of a Roman collection of laws,: rationum,: patrimonii,: omnia maternae hereditatis,.

la:verb:corrumpo.html:
cor-rumpo (conr-), rūpi, ruptum (rumptum), 3, v. a. (orig.,
to break to pieces; hence),
To destroy, ruin, waste, bring to naught (class., but less freq. than in the signif. II.].
Lit.: reliquum frumentum flumine atque incendio corruperunt,: domum et semet igni conrumpunt,; cf.: plura igni,; 92, 8: res familiares,: ungues dentibus,i. e. to bite, (13).—
Trop.: diem,: animo malest: corrupta sum atque absumpta sum,: se suasque spes,: illos dubitando et dies prolatando magnas opportunitates corrumpere,to lose,: consilia,: libertatem,: foedera,: omnem prospectum,—
With regard to the physical or moral quality of an object, to corrupt, mar, injure, spoil, adulterate, make worse, etc. (very freq., and class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.: corrumpitur jam cena,; so, prandium,: conclusa aqua facile conrumpitur,; cf.: aquarum fontes,: corrupitque lacus, infecit pabula leto,: coria igni ac lapidibus,: ne plora, oculos corrumpis,; cf.: ocellos lacrimis,: artus febribus, (20), 117; cf.: stomachum (medicamentum),: umor ex hordeo aut frumento in quandam similitudinem vini corruptus,fermented,: vinum in acorem corrumpitur,.—Poet., without the access. idea of impairing: ebur corrumpitur ostro,is stained,.—
Trop. (so most freq.),
Of personal objects, to corrupt, seduce, entice, mislead: perde rem, Corrumpe erilem filium,; sq.; cf. : me ex amore hujus esse corrumptum,; : mulierem,; cf. feminas,: (vitiosi principes) non solum obsunt, ipsi quod corrumpuntur, sed etiam quod corrumpunt,: quos (milites) soluto imperio, licentia atque lascivia corruperat,; cf. et saep.—
In partic., to gain to one's self by gifts, etc.; to bribe, buy over, etc.
With abl.: aliquem pecuniā,; : auro,: pretio, 25, 72: turpi largitione,: donis,: muneribus, et saep.—
Without abl.: ne alios corrumpas, cum me non potueris,; bis; ; et saep.—
Of things as objects, to corrupt, adulterate, falsify, spoil, mar, etc.: litteras publicas,: tabulas publicas,, § 104; : mores civitatis (opp. corrigere),; : disciplinam,: fides, quam nec cupiditas corrumpat, nec gratia avertat,: totidem generibus corrumpitur oratio, quot ornatur,: nomen eorum paulatim Libyes corrupere,; cf. : multo dolore corrupta voluptas,imbittered,: gratiam,to forfeit,: (littera) continuata cum insequente in naturam ejus corrumpitur,; cf.: oris plurima vitia in peregrinum sonum corrupti,: quamvis sciam non corrumpi in deterius quae aliquando etiam a malis ... fiunt,: ineluctabilis fatorum vis consilia corrumpit,.—*
In partic. (acc. to II. B. b.), to bribe: nutricis fidem,.—Hence, cor-ruptus (conr-, cŏrup-), a, um, P. a., spoiled, marred, corrupted, bad.
Lit.: caelum, Munro ad loc.; cf.: tractus caeli,: aqua corruptior jam salsiorque, Auct. B. Alex. 6 fin.: iter factum corruptius imbri,—
Trop.
Of the forms of words, mutilated, corrupted (opp. integer), .—
Bad, corrupt: quis corruptor juventutis, quis corruptus, qui? etc.,: homines conruptissimi, Dietsch.—Subst.: corrupta, ōrum, n., the spoiled parts (of the body), Cels. praef. § 43.—Adv.: corruptē, corruptly, perversely, incorrectly (very rare): judicare neque depravate neque corrupte, * : pronuntiare verba, ina mutilated manner, .—Comp.: explicare,: intimi libertorum servorumque corruptius quam in privatā domo habiti,; cf. 2, 12 Halm.
